# Case study (portfolio draft): TabPFN vs Pareto/NBD

*Draft for timursalakhetdinov.com. Numbers come from `results/` and are regenerated by `tabpfn-vs-paretonbd report`.*

## Where this comes from

I previously replicated **Abe (2009)**, "Counting Your Customers One by One: A Hierarchical Bayes Extension to
the Pareto/NBD Model", on the CDNOW data. That replication did not include TabPFN.

It answered *can we reproduce the Bayesian model?* This project asks a different question: **now that a
tabular foundation model can learn from labelled examples in context, when is the specialised Bayesian model
still the better tool?**

## What is new in this project

- **A new, independent codebase.** Both Bayesian models are implemented from the original papers.
  - Pareto/NBD MLE is implemented from Schmittlein et al. (1987) and Fader and Hardie (2005, "A Note on Deriving the Pareto/NBD Model and Related Expressions") and reproduces the published CDNOW estimates.
  - Abe HB M1 is implemented as a Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with split-R-hat and ESS diagnostics.
  - On the CDNOW 1/10 sample it recovers the published population means (log λ −3.53 vs −3.58, log μ −3.61 vs
    −3.59). The dropout variance is only weakly determined (ESS ≈ 61), which is disclosed.
- **A forecasting question, not a fit question.** The target is observable, P(no purchase in the next 90 days),
  and not P(alive). The Bayesian models are scored on that probability, derived from the model, not on their
  alive-probability.
- **Temporal honesty.**
  - Forecasts are made at monthly origins with mature labels only.
  - Frozen development and holdout origins.
  - Customer-clustered paired bootstrap.
  - Learning curves over the number of *labelled customers*.
- **A second, richer dataset.** UCI Online Retail II (wholesale, 5,878 customers) is used as the primary benchmark.
  CDNOW is kept as the Bayesian models' "home" dataset.
- **A workbench.** A Streamlit app shows:
  - one customer's history at a past origin;
  - what every model predicted and what actually happened;
  - calibration and ranking views.

## Results

Measured on three untouched holdout origins of Online Retail II (15,433 customer-origin rows). Full tables are in the
README.

- **With the Pareto/NBD's own inputs** (frequency, recency, age), the label-free Pareto/NBD beat TabPFN-3.5 on Brier
  score: 0.169 vs 0.177, difference −0.008 [−0.009, −0.007]. It was also the best-calibrated model.
- **With richer history features**, TabPFN-3.5 tied with the Pareto/NBD, the GLM and tuned LightGBM on Brier (all
  within ±0.0005, intervals include zero). It had the best ranking (PR-AUC 0.858) and the best 90-day count forecast
  (MAE 0.561, significantly better than all others).
- **Labels matter less for TabPFN-3.5.** With 50–250 labelled customers it was the best supervised model by a clear
  margin: Brier 0.190 vs 0.208 (GLM) and 0.239 (LightGBM) at 50 customers.
- **The hierarchical Bayesian model did not converge** on this young, growing customer base (max R-hat 1.48), so it is
  reported as a failure, not scored.

- **On CDNOW**, where the Bayesian models come from, Abe's HB model converged (max R-hat 1.06). On the common
  inputs it was the best model: Brier 0.0968 vs TabPFN-3.5's 0.0980, and count MAE 0.298 vs 0.333. With expanded features
  TabPFN-3.5 edged ahead on Brier (0.0964, +0.0004 [+0.0001, +0.0008] in its favour), while the Bayesian models
  kept the best count forecasts.

## What I learned

- **The information set decides the winner more than the model class does.** On equal inputs, a 1987 model
  with no labels was hard to beat. TabPFN-3.5's advantage appeared when it could use features that the Pareto/NBD
  cannot represent.
- **Small labelled samples are where in-context learning pays off.** Without tuning it beat tuned LightGBM clearly
  below about 500 customers.
- **Dataset drift hurts calibration.** Training on the latest matured origin under a changing inactivity rate
  left TabPFN-3.5 worst-calibrated and 17–20 % short on total purchases. The unsupervised model avoided this because it
  never sees labels.
- **Convergence gates need to be set before the results.** Setting R-hat < 1.1 before holdout scoring made
  excluding Abe HB on Online Retail II a rule, not a judgement call.

## Limits

- One retailer and one period. The three holdout origins overlap in time, so they are not independent.
- No treatment data, so no uplift or ROI claims.
- TabPFN-3.5 weights are under a non-commercial licence. The project code is Apache-2.0.
